title: A shallow copy contains a nested list. Is that inner list duplicated?
back: No. A shallow copy keeps references to nested objects.
explanation: The outer container is new, but its members are referenced. A deep copy recursively copies members, with special handling for recursive structures.

title: Which standard-library collection counts hashable values?
explanation: Counter maps elements to their counts. It is useful for tallies such as status-code frequencies without manually initializing every key.

title: A Python tuple takes a trip through JSON. What comes back by default?
explanation: JSON arrays decode to Python lists. JSON does not preserve every Python type, so a successful round trip does not guarantee the same Python object type.

title: With pathlib, what does the / operator do between path components?
explanation: Path objects can combine a base directory with a relative component using /. Constructing a path does not create the directory or prove the file exists.

title: In Python logging, which is more severe: WARNING or ERROR?
explanation: The standard sequence increases from DEBUG through INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL. Logger and handler thresholds both affect which messages appear.

title: Does calling an async Python function immediately run its body?
back: No. It returns a coroutine object.
explanation: Await the coroutine or schedule it, for example with create_task in a running event loop. Merely creating the coroutine does not execute its body.

title: What is the purpose of a context manager around an acquired resource?
explanation: A with statement calls the context manager’s exit behavior when leaving the block, including exceptional exits. Individual context managers decide which cleanup to perform.

title: What does subprocess.run(..., check=True) do with a nonzero exit code?
explanation: Without check=True, a completed command can return a nonzero status without that exception. A launched process and a successful command are different outcomes.

title: How does Python recommend opening a file for csv.reader?
explanation: The csv module performs its own newline handling. Its documentation recommends newline="" for file objects used by the reader and writer.

title: What makes a Python datetime timezone-aware?
explanation: An aware datetime can locate itself relative to other aware times. A naive datetime does not specify enough timezone information to identify one unambiguous instant.

title: Which Git tool narrows down the commit that introduced a regression?
explanation: Mark known good and bad revisions, then test the selected revisions. Bisect uses binary search to narrow the candidate history; it still needs a meaningful good/bad check.

title: Where can you inspect previous positions of a local Git branch tip?
explanation: Reflogs record local reference updates. They can help locate recent commits after a mistaken reset, but entries expire and are not a substitute for backups.

title: Which diff shows what is staged for your next Git commit?
explanation: A plain git diff compares the working tree with the index. The cached form compares the index with the selected commit, normally HEAD.

title: Does adding a tracked file to .gitignore remove it from Git history?
explanation: Ignore rules apply to intentionally untracked files. They neither erase committed contents nor make a previously exposed secret safe to use.

title: Does a default git stash include ordinary untracked files?
back: No. Use --include-untracked when that is intended.
explanation: The default stash covers tracked modifications. The -u option includes untracked files; ignored files require a different, broader option.

title: What does a database transaction group together?
back: Operations that succeed or fail as a unit.
explanation: BEGIN starts an explicit PostgreSQL transaction block. COMMIT makes its work permanent; ROLLBACK discards the block’s changes.

title: Which join keeps unmatched rows from its left input?
explanation: Matching right-side values are returned where available. When no match exists, columns from the right side are null for that left-side row.

title: WHERE or HAVING: which filters groups after aggregation?
explanation: WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING tests the resulting groups, so aggregate conditions belong there.

title: Does a window function normally collapse several rows into one result row?
back: No. It retains the individual rows.
explanation: Window functions compute over a related set of rows while each output row keeps its identity. An ordinary grouped aggregate typically reduces rows into groups.

title: Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually run the statement?
explanation: ANALYZE obtains real execution information by running the statement. Account for side effects and workload impact before using it on data-changing or expensive statements.

title: Which Kubernetes probe says whether a container is ready to receive traffic?
explanation: Failed readiness removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints for ordinary traffic handling. It does not by itself request the liveness-style container restart.

title: What can protect a slow-starting container from premature liveness checks?
explanation: When configured, a startup probe delays liveness and readiness probing until startup succeeds. Give it a threshold that reflects realistic startup behavior.

title: Does base64-encoding a Kubernetes Secret encrypt it?
explanation: Secret data needs appropriate access controls and encryption configuration. Anyone able to read an encoded value can decode it without a cryptographic key.

title: Where should non-confidential application configuration go in Kubernetes?
explanation: ConfigMaps hold non-confidential configuration that can be consumed as environment variables, arguments, or files. They are not designed to keep secrets confidential.

title: What remains stable while Kubernetes replaces application Pods?
back: A Service can provide a stable access abstraction.
explanation: Pods are temporary and their addresses can change. A Service selects a set of endpoints so clients need not track each replacement Pod directly.

title: Can Kubernetes publish DNS names for Services?
back: Yes. Cluster DNS creates Service records.
explanation: Service naming lets workloads discover services by name. Exact records depend on Service type, namespace, and cluster DNS configuration.

title: Is creating a NetworkPolicy object enough to guarantee enforcement?
back: No. The network implementation must support it.
explanation: Kubernetes requires a network plugin that implements NetworkPolicy. Policy intent and actual traffic enforcement must be checked together.

title: Are all Kubernetes objects namespaced?
explanation: Namespaces partition many resources, such as Pods and Services. Nodes and PersistentVolumes are examples of objects outside an individual namespace.

title: Which controller can run a node-level agent on all eligible Kubernetes nodes?
explanation: DaemonSets are commonly used for per-node logging, storage, or monitoring services. Node selection and scheduling rules determine which nodes are eligible.

title: Which controller gives Pods stable identities for stateful workloads?
explanation: StatefulSets support stable network identities and persistent storage associations. Application data consistency still depends on the application and its storage design.

title: Why bundle preprocessing and an estimator in a scikit-learn Pipeline?
back: To apply the same ordered transformation and estimation steps consistently.
explanation: Pipelines also help cross-validation fit transformations within training folds. Keeping preprocessing outside the split can leak information.

title: What does stratified splitting try to preserve for classification?
back: The relative class frequencies in each split.
explanation: Stratification helps avoid folds with badly distorted class proportions. It does not automatically prevent time leakage or repeated-subject leakage.

title: The same patient appears in several rows. What should a split respect?
explanation: A group-aware split can keep one subject out of both training and test partitions. Random row splitting may test on information about a subject already seen.

title: What does a confusion matrix compare?
explanation: Its cells count class-by-class outcomes. Reading the labels matters because libraries and diagrams can use different axis conventions.

title: Does unsupervised clustering require class labels during fitting?
explanation: Clustering groups observations using structure in their features. The resulting cluster IDs are not automatically meaningful business categories.

title: What do the first PCA components seek to capture?
back: Directions of greatest variance, subject to orthogonality.
explanation: PCA is a linear transformation. High explained variance does not, by itself, mean the retained directions are the most useful for a prediction task.

title: Which split should supply the mean and variance for your feature scaler?
explanation: Fit preprocessing on training data, then transform validation and test data with those learned parameters. Fitting on all rows can contaminate the evaluation.

title: Despite its name, what task is logistic regression commonly used for?
explanation: It models class probabilities and uses a decision rule to predict labels. Linear regression, in contrast, directly predicts a continuous target.

title: What can limiting a decision tree’s depth control?
back: Its complexity and tendency to overfit.
explanation: An unrestricted tree may fit very specific training patterns. Choose depth and other hyperparameters with appropriate validation rather than tuning on the final test set.

title: What is lost when you repeatedly tune against your final test set?
back: Its value as an untouched estimate of generalization.
explanation: Choices become adapted to that set. Use validation or cross-validation for model selection and reserve the final holdout for the final assessment.

title: What does a LangGraph checkpointer preserve?
explanation: Persisted state supports threads, recovery, and inspection. A checkpoint does not independently verify that a model’s claims are correct.

title: What does a LangGraph interrupt let a workflow do?
back: Pause for external input and resume later.
explanation: With persistence configured, an interrupt can surface information to a human or another process. The application still needs to enforce who is authorized to resume it.

title: Why should replayable workflow steps avoid unprotected side effects?
back: A replay can execute work again.
explanation: Use appropriate task boundaries and idempotency for external effects. Durable execution concerns recovery; it does not make every external API call inherently safe to repeat.

title: What is an AI tool’s interface supposed to describe?
back: The operation and its accepted inputs.
explanation: A model can use that description to request an operation. Your implementation is still responsible for validating inputs, enforcing authorization, and reporting failures.

title: Does schema-valid model output prove its fields contain true facts?
explanation: A schema constrains shape and types. Evidence checks and domain validation are still needed for factual claims, identifiers, and consequential decisions.

title: What does MCP help connect in an AI application?
back: Clients with external tools and context through a common protocol.
explanation: Using a standard connection format does not establish trust in each tool or its returned content. Choose access and execution permissions separately.

title: What is context engineering trying to control?
back: The information and tools made available to the model at each step.
explanation: Instructions, retrieved data, state, and available operations all affect an agent’s choices. More context is not automatically more relevant context.

title: Why test an agent’s tool use as well as its final response?
back: A plausible final answer can hide a wrong or unauthorized action.
explanation: Tests can inspect intermediate choices and tool results. The success criteria should cover the task’s behavior, not just whether the final text sounds convincing.

title: Does a GPU health check measure your model’s prediction quality?
back: No. Hardware health and model quality are different measurements.
explanation: DCGM helps monitor and manage GPU infrastructure. Evaluating the model needs representative data and suitable task metrics in addition to healthy hardware.

title: What kind of operational work does DCGM support?
back: Monitoring and managing NVIDIA data center GPUs.
explanation: Health checks, diagnostics, and telemetry support infrastructure operations. Interpret the applicable checks in the context of the GPU, driver, and DCGM version.

title: How wide is an IPv6 address?
explanation: IPv6 expands addressing beyond IPv4’s 32 bits. Address text uses hexadecimal groups, with rules for compressing zeros.

title: Which IPv6 field limits how many forwarding hops a packet can traverse?
explanation: A forwarding node decrements it. The packet is discarded when forwarding would exhaust the limit, helping prevent indefinite circulation.

title: On an IPv4 Ethernet LAN, what does ARP resolve?
back: A protocol address to a local hardware address.
explanation: An ARP exchange can discover the Ethernet address to use on that local link. It does not discover the remote Internet host’s Ethernet address across routers.

title: What makes a DHCP-assigned address temporary?
explanation: A DHCP client renews an address lease according to protocol timing. Address assignment also involves the subnet and configuration offered by the server.

title: What does a DNS record’s TTL tell a cache?
back: How long the cached data can normally be retained.
explanation: Caching reduces repeated lookups, but it means a record change may not be seen immediately by clients using an existing cached answer.

title: In HTTP, what does a safe method mean?
back: Its defined semantics are essentially read-only.
explanation: Safe concerns the requested semantics; logging and other incidental effects may still happen. Safe does not mean encrypted or free of implementation bugs.

title: Does every unsuccessful API response justify an immediate retry loop?
back: No. Decide using the failure and the operation’s semantics.
explanation: A retry policy must account for whether repeating an operation is appropriate. Timing, idempotency, and provider instructions matter as well as the status code.

title: What are Google SRE’s four golden monitoring signals?
explanation: They provide a starting point for understanding service behavior. Instrument the signals that reveal the user impact and resource limits of your own system.

title: Why assign an incident commander during a major outage?
back: To coordinate the response and maintain a shared plan.
explanation: Clear roles help responders work together instead of making conflicting changes. Incident command includes communication and coordination, not doing every repair personally.

title: What should a blameless postmortem investigate?
back: The contributing conditions and opportunities to improve the system.
explanation: Describe what responders knew and how the system behaved. Focusing only on one person’s mistake misses the conditions that can create a repeat incident.

title: The script prints a coroutine instead of collecting a result.
body: A teammate calls fetch_inventory(), an async function, from another async function and prints the returned object. What is the direct missing step?
options: Await the returned coroutine
Wrap the coroutine in str()
Declare fetch_inventory as a global
Add a return type annotation
explanation: Awaiting the coroutine obtains its result and lets its asynchronous body run. Calling an async function alone produces a coroutine object.

title: One quoted field contains a comma. Your split breaks the row.
body: A device inventory uses CSV with quoted fields. Which parser choice understands those quoting rules?
options: Split each row on every comma
Use a CSV reader configured for the file’s dialect
Strip all quotes and split on commas
Assume every row has the same byte length
explanation: CSV has quoting, delimiter, and newline rules. A CSV parser handles those rules; manually splitting on commas does not distinguish data from separators.

title: The API key was committed yesterday. Today you added .gitignore.
body: Has that ignore rule removed the key from existing commits?
options: Yes; ignore rules erase matching history
Yes; a new clone omits ignored history
No; the committed secret still needs incident handling
Only if the file is also removed from the working tree
explanation: Ignore rules do not rewrite committed history. Treat an exposed credential as exposed: revoke or rotate it through the responsible provider and handle repository cleanup separately.

title: The bug appeared somewhere in 200 commits.
body: You have a repeatable check and know one good revision and one bad revision. Which tool can narrow the history efficiently?
options: git blame without a behavior check
git status on the current revision
git remote prune
git bisect
explanation: Bisect selects candidate revisions using binary search between known good and bad points. The repeatable behavior check is what makes each classification meaningful.

title: One transfer contains a debit and a credit.
body: Which database feature helps ensure both changes commit together or neither commits?
options: A separate autocommit for each write
A transaction containing both writes
An index on the account name alone
A read-only view over the final balances
explanation: A transaction groups operations into an atomic unit. Application validation, isolation choices, and error handling still matter, but separate independent commits do not provide the same unit of work.

title: You want a plan without executing a large UPDATE.
body: Which PostgreSQL command form avoids running that UPDATE as part of plan inspection?
options: EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...
EXPLAIN UPDATE ...
UPDATE ... RETURNING *
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE TRUE) UPDATE ...
explanation: EXPLAIN without ANALYZE shows the planned approach. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement to obtain actual execution measurements, including possible side effects.

title: A Pod is running, but its required initialization is unfinished.
body: You want to withhold normal Service traffic until it can serve requests. Which probe is aimed at that decision?
options: A readiness probe
A liveness probe used as the sole traffic signal
An imagePullPolicy setting
A restart policy alone
explanation: Readiness is the traffic-readiness signal. Liveness asks whether a restart is needed; startup probes help protect initialization from early liveness and readiness checks.

title: The policy exists. Traffic still passes.
body: Your cluster uses a network plugin without NetworkPolicy support. Which explanation fits?
options: The API object always enforces itself
Policies only affect traffic before Pod creation
The plugin cannot enforce the policy
A policy in one namespace necessarily isolates every namespace
explanation: A NetworkPolicy requires an implementation that supports enforcement. Successfully storing the object in the API is not proof that the data plane is applying it.

title: The Secret value is base64. A reviewer calls it encrypted.
body: Which response is technically accurate?
options: Base64 protects the value with a secret key
Base64 is reversible encoding; configure real security controls
A Secret is always encrypted at rest without configuration
Namespace separation alone makes it unreadable to administrators
explanation: Base64 is not encryption. Evaluate access rights, encryption at rest, and how the workload obtains and uses the secret.

title: Every eligible node needs the same log collector.
body: Which Kubernetes workload controller is designed for this node-oriented placement?
options: A Job that runs once for the whole cluster
A ClusterIP Service without a workload
A DaemonSet
A ConfigMap containing the agent configuration
explanation: A DaemonSet places a Pod on each eligible node, subject to selectors and scheduling constraints. It fits agents that need a node-local presence.

title: A model recognizes the patient instead of generalizing.
body: Several measurements from the same person were randomly split between training and test sets. What split design addresses that overlap?
options: Keep each person’s rows in one partition
Shuffle rows and keep the existing split
Remove the subject ID after randomly splitting rows
Use more folds while keeping subject overlap
explanation: A group-aware split separates subjects across partitions. Row-level randomness alone cannot stop a model from benefiting from repeated-subject information.

title: The scaler learned from the test set.
body: You fit preprocessing on the full dataset before splitting. Which repair protects the held-out evaluation?
options: Choose the split with the best final test score
Include test labels when fitting the scaler
Fit preprocessing only on training data, then transform the other splits
Fit a different scaler independently to every test batch
explanation: Preprocessing parameters must be learned without the held-out data. A correctly configured pipeline helps apply that separation during validation.

title: 99% accuracy, zero detected failures.
body: Only 1% of examples represent failures. The classifier always predicts normal. What should you examine next?
options: Only the aggregate accuracy
Per-class outcomes, including missed failures
Only the training-set loss
Only the number of model parameters
explanation: Overall accuracy can look high on imbalanced data while the minority class is never found. Inspect a confusion matrix and metrics that reflect the actual costs of errors.

title: The clustering algorithm returned groups 0, 1, and 2.
body: What can you safely conclude from those IDs alone?
options: Cluster 2 is intrinsically higher risk than cluster 1
Cluster 0 always contains invalid observations
The cluster IDs encode universal class meanings
They identify groups; their meaning needs interpretation
explanation: Cluster labels are identifiers, not automatic semantic judgments. Investigate the observations and the algorithm’s assumptions before attaching operational meaning.

title: The agent returned perfect JSON with an invented ticket number.
body: Which missing check addresses the problem?
options: A JSON formatter
A lookup against the authoritative ticket system
A stricter rule that the field must be a string
The model’s self-reported confidence alone
explanation: Structured output constrains representation. Verifying that a ticket exists and that an action is permitted requires checks against the relevant system.

title: A resumed workflow sends the same notification again.
body: Which design change targets accidental repeated external effects?
options: Increase the retry count
Restart the whole graph on every timeout
Use suitable idempotency and durable task boundaries
Assume persistence makes all external calls exactly-once
explanation: Workflow recovery can revisit steps. External effects need explicit repeat-handling and appropriate boundaries; recovery alone does not make each external call idempotent.

title: The agent is about to request a consequential change.
body: Where can a human decision enter a LangGraph flow without discarding its saved state?
options: At an interrupt with persistence configured
Only by discarding and rebuilding the graph
Only after every external effect has completed
By editing the final response after the tool runs
explanation: Interrupts can pause a graph and return information for external review. Configure persistence and enforce authorization around the decision and the later tool execution.

title: The final answer looks right. The tool wrote to the wrong record.
body: Which test would be more informative than checking the final text alone?
options: A final-answer keyword check alone
A tool-call assertion covering the target and resulting effect
A check that the response is valid JSON alone
A check of the prompt token count alone
explanation: Observable tool behavior is part of an agent’s result. Check the actual target, action, and effect, in addition to any final response.

title: All GPU health checks pass. The model fails its evaluation.
body: What follows from these two results?
options: Hardware health guarantees good predictions
The evaluation must be invalid because the GPU is healthy
Higher GPU utilization alone resolves prediction errors
Infrastructure health and model quality require separate investigation
explanation: A hardware diagnostic and a model evaluation answer different questions. Healthy infrastructure can run a poorly trained, misconfigured, or unsuitable model.

title: The DNS record changed, but one client sees the old address.
body: Before assuming the edit failed, which mechanism should you consider?
options: An existing cached answer within its TTL
ARP caches storing the hostname’s DNS records
DHCP rewriting the authoritative DNS record for every lookup
Every lookup necessarily bypassing intermediate caches
explanation: DNS caching can retain an answer until its applicable lifetime expires. Check the actual resolver and record path rather than assuming every client queries the authoritative server on each request.

title: The agent: “I can fix that in one tool call.”
body: The tool call: production.deleteEverything()
prompt: Give an agent a tool boundary you would be comfortable reviewing. What actions deserve an explicit approval step?

title: Agent status: complete.
body: Test status: we have questions.
prompt: Choose one observable behavior that must pass before you accept an agent’s claim of completion.

title: I gave the agent the entire repository.
body: It gave me the entire repository back.
prompt: What is the smallest relevant context for one bounded code change?

title: Added five agents to fix a naming problem.
body: Now we have six naming conventions.
prompt: Which coordination problem appears when multiple agents can change the same files?

title: The response is valid JSON.
body: Unfortunately, reality uses a different schema.
prompt: Which fields in an AI response need to be checked against an authoritative system?

title: Workflow retries: working perfectly.
body: Customer emails sent: 47.
prompt: How would you prevent a retry from duplicating an external effect?

title: Human in the loop.
body: Human currently in another meeting.
prompt: What should a paused workflow show while waiting for an authorized decision?

title: Connected another MCP server.
body: My permissions dialog now has a scroll bar.
prompt: Which tools does this specific task actually require?

title: The branch is called final-final-working.
body: The stash is called emotional support.
prompt: What work belongs in a clear commit instead of an indefinitely hidden stash?

title: Good news: we found the commit.
body: Bad news: the author is me.
prompt: What repeatable check would make a regression easy to locate?

title: “Just a tiny cleanup.”
prompt: How could you divide a change into independently reviewable steps?

title: Added the leaked key to .gitignore.
body: The key: “I’m already in the group chat.”
prompt: Why does an ignore rule not repair a secret already committed to history?

title: Me: I definitely meant to reset that branch.
body: Also me: hello, reflog, my old friend.
prompt: What does your local reflog retain, and why is it not a permanent backup?

title: The JOIN was supposed to find five devices.
body: It introduced every device to every other device.
prompt: What join condition prevents an unintended Cartesian product?

title: COMMIT is a very confident word.
body: ROLLBACK is a very comforting one.
prompt: Where should an all-or-nothing boundary sit in a multi-step database operation?

title: I only wanted to inspect the query.
body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE: I brought receipts. And side effects.
prompt: When does PostgreSQL actually execute the statement during plan inspection?

title: Made a shallow copy of my problems.
body: Now two lists share the same problems.
prompt: Which nested objects are still shared after a shallow copy?

title: My tuple went through JSON.
body: Came back with a list of new priorities.
prompt: Which Python types are not preserved by a default JSON round trip?

title: I called the async function. Nothing happened.
body: The coroutine is waiting for a formal invitation.
prompt: What is the difference between creating a coroutine and awaiting or scheduling it?

title: The file definitely exists.
body: In my other working directory.
prompt: What path and working directory is your process actually using?

title: Turned on DEBUG to find one error.
body: Found the entire life story of the application.
prompt: Which log fields would help diagnose a problem without collecting unnecessary sensitive data?

title: Scheduled for 9 AM.
body: A bold statement without a timezone.
prompt: What information turns a local clock reading into an unambiguous instant?

title: The container is alive.
body: Its readiness for responsibility is another matter.
prompt: Why are liveness and readiness separate signals?

title: Security plan: base64.
body: That’s a costume, not a vault.
prompt: What protects secret data besides changing its representation?

title: It worked before the config change.
body: The config change: “Why are you looking at me?”
prompt: How can you trace the configuration version associated with a failure?

title: Named the namespace temporary.
body: It has survived three reorganizations.
prompt: Who owns the resources in a namespace, and how is their lifecycle managed?

title: One tiny monitoring agent per node.
body: The agents have formed a neighborhood.
prompt: Which nodes should actually receive a node-level agent?

title: Changed DNS and refreshed immediately.
body: The cache has chosen to remember our past.
prompt: What TTL and resolver behavior explain an old answer after a change?

title: The firewall policy looks beautiful in Git.
body: Packets have not read the repository.
prompt: What observation proves that the intended policy is enforced in the data plane?

title: Ran out of IPv4 addresses in the lab.
body: IPv6 has entered the chat with 128 bits.
prompt: How does IPv6’s address size compare with IPv4’s?

title: I asked ARP for the remote server’s MAC.
body: ARP: “I work in this neighborhood.”
prompt: Which link-layer address is needed when sending toward a remote network?

title: The workstation says it owns this address.
body: DHCP says it’s a rental agreement.
prompt: What happens when an address lease needs to be renewed?

title: Our model predicts the test set perfectly.
body: It should. We introduced them during training.
prompt: How could information from a held-out set enter preprocessing or model selection?

title: Accuracy: 99%.
body: Detected incidents: please don’t ask.
prompt: What do the minority-class recall and confusion matrix reveal that overall accuracy hides?

title: The algorithm discovered three clusters.
body: Management has already given them personalities.
prompt: What evidence would justify a meaningful label for an unsupervised cluster?

title: Spent the weekend on a complex model.
body: The baseline brought a folding chair and won.
prompt: What simple comparison helps show whether added model complexity is useful?

title: GPU utilization: 100%.
body: Useful progress: still under investigation.
prompt: Which application and infrastructure metrics distinguish busy hardware from successful work?

title: The monitoring dashboard is green.
body: The users would like to appeal.
prompt: Which measurements reflect the experience of actual requests?

title: Joined the incident bridge to help.
body: Now I’m the incident commander.
prompt: What roles and shared state would help responders coordinate?

title: Root cause: “human error.”
body: The humans would like a better system.
prompt: What contributing system conditions belong in a blameless incident review?
